De Roxham à la terre d’asile : un chemin: From Roxham to a Land of Asylum: A Precarious Path
« Ta famille compte sur toi pour survivr: “Your family is counting on you to survive. There is no state over there”
Les différents visages du chemin Roxham: The many faces of Roxham Road, in illustration: the bus that carries asylum seekers who cross at Roxham Road; a tribute to Fritznel Richard, an asylum seeker who lost his life in the forest along the road; a fence representing the border and the asylum seekers’ point of entry; a young family of asylum seekers; the Roxham Road intersection in winter; a young immigrant woman showing a photo of her children, whom she left behind before coming to Canada. Illustration: Nia E-K
Le 23 décembre 2022, une tempête est ann: On December 23, 2022, a storm is forecast. Nothing unusual for most Quebecers. The heat is on, the doors are shut, and people wait for it to pass. But for Fritznel Richard, an asylum seeker from Haiti, this storm will prove fatal. In the days before, faced with severe hardship, he wants to leave Quebec. He wants to be reunited with his wife and child in the United States and decides to go back on foot, through the forest that runs alongside Roxham Road. On January 4, two weeks later, he is found not far away, dead from the cold.
Comme lui, des milliers de demandeurs d’: Like him, thousands of asylum seekers must cope with financial insecurity and social isolation that can push them to turn back.
Pour mieux comprendre leur situation, no: To better understand their situation, we spoke with Francesca, Jonathan and Slandie, who all three crossed the Canada-U.S. border at Roxham Road. They told their stories for the first time, alongside Frantz André, a member of the Comité d’action des personnes sans statut (CAPSS).
En 2012, Haïti conclut une entente avec: In 2012, Haiti signed an agreement with Brazil that allowed its citizens to obtain Brazilian visas free of charge. Brazil’s textile industry was booming at the time, and the country needed labour. That is where Francesca’s migration journey begins.
La jeune femme de 27 ans fond en larmes: The 27-year-old breaks down in tears as she recalls the trip. “My grandmother had to sell her house so I could leave,” she begins. “The visa was supposed to be free, but we still had to pay a sum to the person handling the file. In total, going to Brazil cost me about US$6,000,” she says, emotional.
Sur place, elle gagne sa vie en travaill: There, she earned a living working in a butcher shop and braiding hair. It is also where she gave birth to her first child. After two years in Brazil, she set out for Canada with her toddler on her back.
« J’ai quitté le Brésil avec mon bébé de: “I left Brazil with my 10-month-old baby. I took a bus to Peru, and then to Colombia. From there, we took dugout canoes,” says Francesca. “There are people who died. We crossed the jungle on foot in Colombia. You have to be physically fit to walk three days and three nights, to cover distance. Then our group made its way to Panama, avoiding the regular roads, always through the forest.”
En tout, la jeune femme va passer 6 mois: In all, the young woman would spend six months on the road and cross 10 countries before reaching the United States with her baby. Within her group, rules took hold: “If you have money and you buy yourself a bottle of water, you have to buy one for everyone. That way, when you get tired, you have someone to lean on,” the young mother explains. Danger was constant: “On that road, there are people who are raped, there are people who get robbed, there are all kinds of things. But afterward, you have to keep going.” Francesca also had to buy the services of smugglers at a steep price. “We pay huge amounts and yet people die along the way,” she laments.
Arrivée aux États-Unis, elle emménage ch: Once in the United States, she moved in with an acquaintance and lived through abusive situations. In 2017, she decided to go to Canada, via Roxham Road. Today, she works in private seniors’ residences as a personal support worker.
Elle est actuellement sans statut, ayant: She is currently without status, having received a negative response to her asylum claim. She is now waiting for the answer to her humanitarian application. She also hopes to benefit from a federal program to regularize people without immigration status, which is expected to come into effect in the coming months. Although the details of the program have not yet been released, the government is considering regularizing 500,000 people without status in Canada.
Francesca redoute la déportation. En eff: Francesca fears deportation. Indeed, many Haitians are harassed and kidnapped on their return by criminals who assume they have accumulated large sums of money. “I can’t go back to Haiti,” she says, visibly terrified. “Last week, a woman was tortured and killed in a public square for speaking to a police officer,” she says between sobs.
Une jeune femme immigrée montre la photo: A young immigrant woman shows a photo of her children, whom she left behind before coming to Canada. Illustration: Nia E-K
Le récit du parcours de Francesca ne lai: Francesca’s story does not leave Slandie unmoved. She is worried about her brother, who has just left Brazil to try his luck on the road as well. “I hear this, and it scares me,” she says.
« L’hiver qui arrive est stressant, loin: “The winter that’s coming is stressful, far from my family,” the young woman adds softly, pressing her hands together. She is visibly embarrassed, but a smile lights up her face.
Elle raconte qu’en Haïti, une fois sa dé: She says that in Haiti, once she had made her decision, her family helped her leave the country. She obtained a U.S. visa and landed in Florida, after leaving her three children with her parents. Within days, with the help of friends, she managed to reach Canada via Roxham Road.
Sandlie est ensuite confrontée à une sér: Slandie then faced a series of administrative hurdles, including receiving a hearing date without knowing how to prepare and dealing with a court-appointed lawyer who, according to her, did not handle her file properly. Meeting Frantz André, however, marked a turning point in her migration journey. Today, after four years in Canada, she has just obtained permanent residence. However, she still cannot bring her three children here. Although they have received their Quebec Selection Certificate, they do not yet have permanent residence.
Slandie jongle avec deux emplois : prépo: Slandie juggles two jobs: home care personal support worker by day and security guard on weekends. She says she experiences racism at work. “Some elderly people told me that working hard is nothing for a Black person, given our past as slaves. Others accused me of theft. Others still leave money lying under their bed to see if I’ll touch it. If you’re accused, it’s your word against theirs,” she says. “We aren’t protected against these accusations in placement agencies,” she laments.
Ces emplois lui permettent de soutenir s: These jobs allow her to support loved ones who stayed back home. “Your family is counting on you to survive. There is no state over there”, she explains. Corruption and kidnapping are commonplace. “Even in the banks, when you send money, there are employees who are in cahoots with the bandits. They spot the people receiving the transfers so they can take them hostage.”
En repensant à Haïti et à son parcours,: Looking back on Haiti and her journey, she says she has no regrets. Yet here, loneliness weighs on her. “I miss my children. I haven’t made any friends. I work a lot to forget my pain. Sometimes I come home and I drink alcohol. I know it’s not good, and I put on some music, I dance and I cry.”
On sent malgré tout chez elle une grande: Still, a great determination comes through when she speaks about the years ahead. “When I have my children with me, I’ll go to school to become a nurse. I want to make them proud,” she says.
Jonathan est lui aussi passé par le chem: Jonathan also came through Roxham Road, in 2017. “In Haiti, girls were getting kidnapped, there were gangs shooting at each other,” he recalls. “My father didn’t want to let us go. It was when my brother insisted that he took me aside and gave me his blessing for our journey.” Jonathan left everything behind at 22 and reached Florida with his brother, a short stop before Canada.
Une fois sur place, il se voit refuser s: Once here, his asylum claim was rejected. However, since 2019 and a moratorium establishing an administrative deferral of removals (ADR), a temporary ban on deportations to Haiti has allowed him to stay in the country. He also holds a work permit that he renews every year.
Sa demande d’asile ayant été refusée, le: With his asylum claim refused, the 27-year-old lives without status in Quebec. In Haiti, he was about to finish his pharmacy studies. In Montréal, he is a security guard at a university. “This job reminds me that I was in the third year of my bachelor’s degree,” he says nostalgically.
Il attend maintenant la réponse à sa dem: He is now waiting for the answer to his humanitarian application, which would give him refugee status. He, too, hopes to resume his studies here. Does he regret coming to Canada? “Sometimes I do, but when I see the situation back home, I tell myself that, in the end, it’s a good thing. And when I talk to my parents, they help me hang on.”
Les demandeurs d’asile ont accès à des a: Asylum seekers have access to legal aid lawyers to argue their cases. Francesca, Slandie and Jonathan believe, however, that this help has not always worked in their favour.
Slandie décrit son avocat comme quelqu’u: Slandie describes her lawyer as disengaged, someone who thought she would not get permanent residence. He allegedly changed his behaviour when Frantz André got involved in the case. After three summonses, the young woman ultimately obtained her permanent residence.
Jonathan estime pour sa part que l’aide: For his part, Jonathan believes that legal aid and the complex administrative process asylum seekers face harmed his case. He notes that legal aid lawyers are overloaded and do not have time to provide appropriate support to their clients. “Before we hired a private lawyer, my brother and I were passed on to three lawyers in three years. They often changed positions. We felt our file was being botched and that they didn’t really have time for us. It’s as if they were overloaded,” he recalls. Jonathan met Frantz André through one of his aunts. André put him in touch with a private lawyer. “I didn’t know I could do that, I had simply been advised to go with legal aid,” the young man laments.
Dave, un réfugié haïtien, est également: Dave, a Haitian refugee, has been through this too. “A lot of people told us that public-sector lawyers didn’t have time for us and didn’t give a damn about us,” he says. That is what led him to hire a private lawyer. He says, however, that he saw no real difference in how his case was handled. After three years of waiting, he obtained a Quebec Selection Certificate. “I think it would make more sense to have lawyers who have lived through the same thing as us, to better help asylum seekers and understand them,” says Dave. The experience prompted him to begin studying law.
Une fois la frontière canado-américaine: Once they have crossed the Canada-U.S. border at Roxham Road, migrants automatically become asylum seekers. A regular return to the United States then becomes impossible. Once in Canada, they must obtain a Refugee Protection Claimant Document (RPCD), which entitles them to free health care and a work permit renewable annually. But the procedures can take a long time.
« Ces derniers temps, la priorité pour l: “Lately, priority for RPCDs and work permits has been given to Ukrainian refugees. For asylum seekers who were already in the country, the wait is longer,” says Frantz André. According to him, Fritznel Richard suffered from this situation. “I know people who have been waiting for their work permit for more than a year,” he says.
Par ailleurs, le renouvellement doit êtr: In addition, renewal must be done four months before the document’s expiry date. Yet processing times are often longer. “Legally, an asylum seeker can keep working with an expired RPCD if they can prove they sent in the renewal. But employers don’t take that into account.” Slandie says she was once fired 15 days before her document expired. She had, in fact, already applied for renewal.
« Ils sont laissés à eux-mêmes. Les orga: “They’re left to fend for themselves. Organizations aren’t funded to provide a service to this population,” argues Stephan Reichhold of the Table de concertation des organismes au service des personnes réfugiées et immigrantes. The situation is all the more difficult because, he says, asylum seekers are not eligible for the services other newcomers are entitled to.
Selon Francesca, Slandie et Jonathan, la: According to Francesca, Slandie and Jonathan, meeting Frantz André allowed them to get out of what they describe as administrative chaos. “After God, there’s Mr. Frantz!” exclaims Slandie. “He’s the only one who helped us.”
Le porte-parole du Comité d’action des p: The spokesperson for the Comité d’action des personnes sans statut (CAPSS) indeed does not count his hours. He estimates he has followed 425 cases since November 2021. Whether it’s submitting work permit applications, filling out asylum claimant documents, preparing exiles to answer immigration officers’ questions or lending them a hand in difficult moments, his tasks are many. He regularly asks governments to improve the services offered to asylum seekers and to cancel the <l1>Safe Third Country Agreement</l1>, which, he says, “pushes these seekers of a new life to take risks, even to the point of losing their lives.” This Canada-U.S. agreement means that once asylum seekers are taken in by Canada, they can no longer legally return to the United States.
Selon M. André, de nombreux exilés souff: According to Mr. André, many exiles suffer from trauma. Psychosocial resources and support are not enough to meet the high demand. “There isn’t enough support. Even as a Quebecer or a Haitian living in Quebec, we don’t have enough. Imagine what it’s like for asylum seekers!” he exclaims.
Durant notre rencontre, l’écoute et l’éc: During our meeting, listening and dialogue allowed the asylum seekers to open up in a caring space, they tell us. They say they opened up for the first time. “I always hid my story, I was afraid of being judged,” admits Francesca.
Dave, lui, a trouvé plus de soutien. Lui: Dave, for his part, found more support. He and his brother attended a school where they were able to socialize, and their parents found support by going to church. He thinks newcomers would need a workshop once a month to socialize, network and learn about the resources available to them. He adds that it is necessary to offer computer literacy services.
Francesca, Slandie et Jonathan souhaiten: Francesca, Slandie and Jonathan want more community representatives who know the Haitian reality to be able to accompany asylum seekers. They also believe that creating spaces for psychological support is essential. They would also like more support from the Haitian diaspora. “It’s as if they don’t want to associate with asylum seekers and people who don’t have regular status,” says Francesca, who reiterates that she can count only on Mr. André’s help.
« À un téléphone près, je suis disponibl: “I’m just a phone call away,” the latter tells his protégés with a smile. The counsellor dips into his own savings to help asylum seekers. It is also at his own expense that he will travel to Florida to bring Fritznel Richard’s ashes to his wife, Guenda Filius. “I didn’t want her to receive his ashes in a box by FedEx. That’s not humane,” he tells us a few days before his departure. But he is stretched to the limit; he would like to hire staff and offer more services to asylum seekers. The counsellor is also in the process of creating a charitable organization that will help him obtain funding for the Comité d’actions des personnes sans statut (CAPSS).
L’autobus qui transporte les demandeurs: The bus that carries asylum seekers to Saint-Bernard-de-Lacolle. Illustration: Nia E-K
Nous nous sommes rendus sur le chemin Ro: We went to Roxham Road to speak with Jean-Philippe, who lives near the border. In 2022, he worked for four months for an agency responsible for receiving people intercepted there by the RCMP.
Nous découvrons que le chemin, bien qu’i: We discover that the road, though irregular, is well marked. There is no border post here, to be sure, but there are surveillance cameras that film every walker. A helicopter regularly crosses the sky, its passes more frequent since Fritznel Richard’s death. Facing the forest he tried to cross to return to the United States, along this small country road, nothing recalls that he lost his life in these woods; no plaque commemorates Fritznel Richard’s memory.
Au point de passage exact entre les deux: At the exact crossing point between the two countries, prefab units have been set up. This is where the exiles wait before being taken to the first reception centre, where they are identified. “We could house up to 150 new people a day at the camp,” Jean-Philippe says. Locals are familiar with these operations. “The RCMP officers, I say hi to them, they say hi to me (…) I see them as neighbours, it’s part of the landscape,” says our host.
Le 27 décembre dernier, ce sont toutefoi: On December 27, however, it was Sûreté du Québec (SQ) officers who showed up at his door, looking for Fritznel Richard. After searching his property, they went to the neighbours’ homes. “I think if it had been a little girl from around here, people would have mobilized more,” Jean-Philippe says regretfully.
Le centre d’accueil est situé à cinq min: The reception centre is five minutes away by road, and the exiles stay there for a maximum of four days before being taken in by relatives or placed in hotel rooms by immigration services. Jean-Philippe had to see to their basic needs: toiletries, bedding and food.
« J’avais l’impression d’être la premièr: “I felt like I was the first person answering their questions,” the young man says. “Because when they come through Roxham Road, they’re placed under arrest by the RCMP, there’s no care given at that place,” he explains. Then Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) officers take over. Photos, fingerprints, identification number – the process is carried out by uniformed staff. “Sometimes there were people who were really scared of that,” Jean-Philippe recalls. According to him, these procedures make the people they serve anonymous. “You don’t know what their names are,” he says. “Staff use the term ‘AS,’ for ‘asylum seeker.’ I preferred to call them ‘users,’” he says of the approach he favoured to avoid reducing them to their experience.
L’ex-employé évoque ensuite des difficul: The former employee then mentions recruitment and logistical difficulties. “That’s why I left. I found it too hard not having the resources to do the job,” he says. He also decries the staff’s lack of training. “Few people worked there out of vocation. That could lead to somewhat harsher treatment of certain clients, something that could be put down to a lack of love, quite simply. Some wore the hat of a prison guard more than the hat of someone who’s there to do humanitarian work.”
Selon lui, l’accueil des demandeurs d’as: In his view, the reception of asylum seekers would be better entrusted to the CBSA rather than the RCMP. “The first face they’d see would be that of people trained in welcoming.” He also calls for more resources and support. “If we let these people in, we have to support them and give them resources to start their lives,” he says.
Un hommage à Fritznel Richard, un demand: A tribute to Fritznel Richard, an asylum seeker who lost his life in the forest along Roxham Road. Illustration: Nia E-K
Fritznel Richard, lui, n’a pas eu cette: Fritznel Richard, for his part, was not so lucky. A final tribute was held for him on January 22. Family and friends gathered to honour his memory. His wife, Guenda Filius, attended the ceremony by videoconference, her young child on her lap. Several members of Montréal’s Haitian community were also there. Magnus Poirier funeral home covered the cost of the ceremony. Jacques Laurent, director of the Montréal-Nord funeral home, is also from the Haitian community. He didn’t hesitate to help. “Unfortunately, there always has to be a Jesus Christ.
C’est Fritznel qui a été crucifié pour s: Fritznel is the one who was crucified to save other migrants, so I think it will bear fruit. But I think there will always be things like this,” he continues. “It takes this kind of unfortunate event to give meaning to life. I would like everyone to become aware of what’s happening, ask questions, not be afraid to get informed, because we have the right to do so. In the best of worlds, just ask people to be careful and to live by our national motto in Haiti: Unity makes strength,” he concludes.
Le 24 janvier dernier, une quinzaine d’o: On January 24, some fifteen organizations that welcome asylum seekers joined their voices to call for more funding, saying the community sector is in a “crisis,” with teams that are “on the verge of exhaustion.” To be able to meet demand, the organizations are asking for more resources. They also want stronger legal support services, as well as the repeal of a 1996 government decision that limits asylum seekers’ access to public services.
Haïti est considéré par les Nations unie: The United Nations considers Haiti to be going through one of the worst humanitarian and human rights crises. The country has also been subject to economic sanctions from the Canadian government and other countries since November 10, 2022, the date the Regulations Implementing the United Nations Resolution on Haiti came into force.
L’entente sur les tiers pays sûrs est un: The Safe Third Country Agreement is a Canada-U.S. accord that requires migrants to claim asylum in the first safe country they set foot in. In practical terms, this means that those who pass through or live in the United States are turned back at Canadian border crossings. However, the agreement, which is being challenged in court, does not apply to migrants who use crossings deemed irregular, such as Roxham Road.
Interrogé au sujet des délais de traitem: Asked about processing times for asylum seekers’ files, the Canadian government’s Department of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship said it introduced a new asylum claim method on September 13, 2022. According to the department, “the new application platform helps make the registration and intake process more efficient.” It also says that on November 16, 2022, it implemented “a temporary public policy that allows asylum seekers to quickly obtain open work permits, which lets them access the Canadian labour market sooner.”
Le ministère indique également que le go: The department also says the federal government paid nearly $698 million to Quebec in 2021-2022 to enable the province to provide settlement and integration services, including to asylum seekers.
Au sujet de l’entente sur les tiers pays: On the Safe Third Country Agreement, the department confirms its intention to maintain the accord between Canada and the United States. “We continue to work with our American counterparts so that the Safe Third Country Agreement remains a humane and fair approach to handling asylum claims between our two countries,” the department said.
